source.title: Polysemanticity or Polysemy? Lexical Identity Confounds Superposition Metrics

page_placements.theme: Apparent polysemanticity often reflects one coherent shared or related feature

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that standard polysemanticity measurements can mistake shared word-form signals for superposition, and reports results that refine that interpretation. It does not measure the claimed proportions of poles with one or two jobs, test explanation predictions on held-out activations, or test the specific other versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron-overlap, sense-selectivity, probing, ablation, SAE, and downstream results related to polysemanticity, but none tests the specific claim versions: it does not audit named jobs per pole or assess whether explanations predict activations on examples they were not written from. The reported results are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper measures lexical-identity confounds in neuron and SAE overlap metrics: overlap from same word with different sense versus different word with same meaning, sense-selectivity, probing, ablation, SAE collisions and downstream editing. It does not audit how many jobs each neuron pole has (V1/V2). It does not examine InceptionV1, pose or recursive generalization (V3), architecture or tool effects on interpretability (V4), or neuron attribution graphs (V5). It does not score explanations against held-out activations (V6/V7). Its thesis is that apparent polysemanticity is often a single word-form job rather than superposition. That is thematically close to V3, but it is in language-model MLP neurons, not the canonical vision examples V3 names. So no version is tested, and the findings go to fits_no_version. The reader's T5 overstates it: the paper makes no specific argument against any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a substantial portion of what metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition. Shared word form produces more neuron overlap than shared meaning across nine models. The confound propagates into SAEs, sits in a compact removable subspace, and causes collateral damage in editing. They explicitly do not deny that genuine superposition exists.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a factorial decomposition of word-form and meaning overlap, SSI-based neuron classification, probing, mean-ablation, and downstream evaluations. It is not the claimed audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles and does not test explanations against held-out activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The lexical contribution varies by layer and model: it generally decreases with depth, with different trajectories across architectures. The reported SL–PS gap is larger for nouns than verbs; changing the Wu-Palmer threshold from 0.35 to 0.65 does not change the condition ordering. Dataset and architecture are also varied.

fits_no_version.finding: Across nine transformers (110M–70B), inputs with the same word but different senses produce more MLP neuron overlap than inputs with different words but the same meaning. Rlex stays above zero at all layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Much measured neuron polysemanticity in language models reflects a single shared word-form feature rather than superposition of unrelated concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Form detectors are mostly sense-blind (67.3%). Sense-blind neurons encode word form (about 85%) but not sense (about 42%). Sense-selective neurons are under about 1–2% of neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons flagged as polysemantic for homonyms often have one coherent job (word identity), analogous to the essay's 'shared feature' reading.

fits_no_version.finding: 18–36% of GPT-2 and Pythia-410M SAE features active on polysemous words are sense-blind. A 4× larger dictionary does not reduce this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features inherit the lexical-identity confound, independent of dictionary size.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating sense-selective neurons affects sense processing much more than ablating sense-blind neurons. Filtering to sense-selective neurons improves WSD and ROME edit selectivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sense-selective and sense-blind neurons play distinct causal roles in sense processing.

record.problems: The authors note that absolute ablation effects are small (<3 perplexity points) and that the 57% confound ratio applies only to polysemous inputs. The corrected score requires sense labels. Some downstream results do not state the model in the main text; several detailed layer results are presented in tables or figures rather than summarized numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The per-layer Rlex values for all models in Appendix B.1, per-layer SSI fractions in Table 7, detailed SAE layer-by-dictionary collision values in Table 8, and full LIS dose-response values in Table 10 are not all separate rows. They are omitted to avoid duplicating numerous layer-specific values; summary rows retain the stated ranges and key contrasts. Figure-only condition trajectories and further appendix robustness results are also omitted.

untested.parts: All: no audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of the share with one or two jobs.
All: no per-pole job shares in any model. The cross-model results concern lexical overlap only.
All: no InceptionV1 or vision neurons, no pose features, no recursive-generalization analysis.
All: no test of whether better tools or architectures raise the share of interpretable neurons.
All: no neuron-based attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
All: no held-out prediction test of explanations. The single SAE feature (#5132) whose label mismatches its firing is anecdotal and concerns an SAE feature, not a neuron.
All: no simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study does not cite the essay. It is not an original source. The 70B result is NF4-quantized, and neuron classification and causal results stop at 13B.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the share of neuron poles with one main job, two related jobs, or unexplained jobs; does not conduct the Qwen3-32B audit.
Tests lexical-versus-semantic overlap across models, but not whether the claimed one-job/two-job/unexplained shares hold across models, dense and MoE architectures, or trillion-parameter scales.
Does not test the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, or recursive generalization.
Does not test the proposed architecture/tool explanation for late-layer interpretability or the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons or compare them with replacement models and reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: It bears on how polysemanticity is measured in LM neurons, but does not test or use any version of the claim.

tranche.reason: The paper tests lexical-identity confounds in polysemanticity and overlap metrics. It does not audit neuron job shares (V1/V2), the canonical vision neurons (V3), tools/architecture (V4), neuron circuits (V5) or explanation scoring (V6/V7). This is a related but different construct, so it fits no version.

source_check.notes: The sense-blind/selective shares, probing and reclassification results are GPT-2 only. Neuron classification and causal experiments use models up to 13B, while the PS > SYN ordering covers all nine models up to 70B. r22 rests on a paper that contradicts itself: B.3 says <1% in all models, but the Table 7 caption gives Pythia-1B layer 0 at 1.80%. The closest version is V3 (apparent polysemanticity as a coherent feature), but the paper studies metric confounds, not the canonical neurons.

statements.correction: PS > SYN neuron overlap in all nine models (110M-70B). On GPT-2: 67.3% of form detectors are sense-blind (SSI < 0.5) and 0.1% are sense-selective. Sense-selective neurons (SSI > 2) are under 1% at every layer in the 12-layer models (Table 7). The Table 7 caption gives Pythia-1B layer 0 at 1.80%. At SSI > 1.5, under 2%. Neuron classification is run only on models up to 13B.
statements.problem: The first sentence (PS > SYN across nine transformers, 110M-70B) is right. The 67.3% sense-blind figure is for GPT-2 only, but the statement places it right after the nine-model sentence without naming GPT-2. '1-2%' mixes the SSI > 2 result (<1%; Pythia-1B layer 0 at 1.80%) with the SSI > 1.5 result (<2%). Neuron classification covers models up to 13B only.
